selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Personal & Professional Development
selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

provenance.reviewNote: CP256: read the selected text and current course evidence in full. The concise cached description makes supported subject/method claims, with no unsupported disciplinary or project guarantee. Displayed text retained unchanged; source provenance recorded.

selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Research Methods & Statistics
selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Research Methods & Statistics introduces research design, operationalisation, measurement, sampling, surveys and experiments. Students study descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression using R and R Commander. A group project develops a research plan and instruments, collects and analyses data, and reports findings under research-ethics and privacy requirements.

provenance.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Revised the description to retain supported academic scope and activities without superseded or unsupported details.

selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Building with Nature
selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Introduces the sustainable engineering approach of working with natural processes for flood protection, land reclamation and port development. Covers history and principles of ecosystem‑based design, explores case studies and includes guest lectures and field excursions.

provenance.reviewNote: CP077: complete selected official description read against current course evidence. Retain accurate overview without extra methods, depth or equivalence inferred.

selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Living with Water
selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Studies water risks and opportunities in deltas, using Zeeland as a central case. Flooding, freshwater scarcity, salinisation, subsidence and pollution are connected to infrastructure, history, governance, law and justice. Students evaluate engineered and nature-based responses, then apply these ideas through site-based inquiry and a project on delta adaptation.

provenance.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Revised the description to retain supported academic scope and activities without superseded or unsupported details.

selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Governance of Sustainability
selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.text: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.

provenance.reviewNote: CP256: read the selected text and current course evidence in full. The concise cached description makes supported subject/method claims, with no unsupported disciplinary or project guarantee. Displayed text retained unchanged; source provenance recorded.

selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Ecosystems Uncovered: How Nature Works
selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Focuses on basic principles of ecology. Studies how environmental conditions affect organisms and examines ecological principles governing individuals, populations, communities and ecosystems, including ecological modelling and applied case studies.

provenance.reviewNote: CP320 reviewed the complete displayed description against current official course description and substantive course evidence. Text retained.

selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Sustainability Essentials I
selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Introduces sustainability through planetary boundaries and scientific tools for understanding human impacts on Earth systems. Students interpret graphs and uncertainty, build simple dynamic models, and study chemical and physical principles relevant to climate, energy and materials. A laboratory project makes and tests starch-based biopolymers.

provenance.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Revised the description to retain supported academic scope and activities without superseded or unsupported details.

selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Sustainability Essentials II
selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Develops physical-science foundations for sustainability through waves, chemistry and materials science. Reflective work and a project apply these topics to analysing greenwashing.

provenance.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Retained the existing description as a faithful account; updated its source provenance.

selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Climate Change
selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.

provenance.reviewNote: CP256: read the selected text and current course evidence in full. The concise cached description makes supported subject/method claims, with no unsupported disciplinary or project guarantee. Displayed text retained unchanged; source provenance recorded.

selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Renewable System Design
selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Teaches assessment of energy usage patterns and strategies for reducing consumption or transitioning to cleaner energy. Explores solar, wind and bioenergy solutions and includes technical and economic analysis; students deliver a report and presentation to a partner company.

provenance.reviewNote: CP256: read the selected text and current course evidence in full. The concise cached description makes supported subject/method claims, with no unsupported disciplinary or project guarantee. Displayed text retained unchanged; source provenance recorded.

selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Modern History
selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.

provenance.reviewNote: CP071: read this complete displayed description and current course evidence. Retain accurate concise subject/method scope; no inferred extra topics, assessment or disciplinary equivalence. Official description retained verbatim.

selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Ethics
selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Ethics examines moral reasoning through historical and contemporary theories and close philosophical reading. Students study utilitarianism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics, alongside Nietzsche, Murdoch and Nagel. Reflection and research essays develop interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.

provenance.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Revised the description to retain supported academic scope and activities without superseded or unsupported details.

selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Introduction to Sociology
selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.

provenance.reviewNote: CP071: read this complete displayed description and current course evidence. Retain accurate concise subject/method scope; no inferred extra topics, assessment or disciplinary equivalence. Official description retained verbatim.

selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.

provenance.reviewNote: CP256: read the selected text and current course evidence in full. The concise cached description makes supported subject/method claims, with no unsupported disciplinary or project guarantee. Displayed text retained unchanged; source provenance recorded.

selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Social Movements & Environmental Justice
selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement.

provenance.reviewNote: CP071: read this complete displayed description and current course evidence. Retain accurate concise subject/method scope; no inferred extra topics, assessment or disciplinary equivalence. Official description retained verbatim.

selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.text: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory studies civil society through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial perspectives. Topics include trust, social capital, public spheres, solidarity, social movements and civil repair. An experience report connects engagement or observation to course concepts, while an individual project uses theoretical and empirical sources to analyse a civil-society organisation, movement or initiative.

selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.text: The Art of Rhetorical Communication develops rhetorical analysis, academic writing and oral presentation. Students examine classical Western roots and the canons of rhetoric, and learn to construct, organise and support persuasive arguments. Historical and contemporary examples connect rhetorical theory with practical communication.

provenance.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Retained the existing description as a faithful account; updated its source provenance.

selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Style & Meaning
selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Style & Meaning studies stylistics: how linguistic choices produce meaning and interpretive effects, principally in literary texts and also in nonfiction. Students connect grammar, discourse and cognition with interpretation through frameworks for dialogue, narration, modality, deixis and text worlds. Analysis exercises lead to an original research-supported stylistic analysis.

provenance.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Revised the description to retain supported academic scope and activities without superseded or unsupported details.

selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Communicating the Climate Crisis
selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Examines how the climate crisis is communicated and contested. Analyzes texts, films, exhibitions, protest art, slogans and social media alongside theory and case studies, teaching students to dissect arguments and culminating in a project where students enter the debate.

provenance.reviewNote: CP071: read this complete displayed description and current course evidence. Retain accurate concise subject/method scope; no inferred extra topics, assessment or disciplinary equivalence. Official description retained verbatim.

selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Persuasive Communication
selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Persuasive Communication studies persuasion through communication studies, social psychology and ethical analysis. Students examine framing, argumentation, cognitive shortcuts and verbal and nonverbal communication. Community-engaged projects develop communication encouraging sustainable and circular lifestyles, while an individual research paper evaluates selected persuasion tools.

provenance.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Revised the description to retain supported academic scope and activities without superseded or unsupported details.

selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Introduction to Western Art History
selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Introduction to Western Art History surveys Western art from late-medieval and Renaissance painting to contemporary practice. Students relate artists, styles and movements to social, religious, political and cultural change. Close examination of paintings develops visual analysis, while a term paper combines study of a painting on location with art-historical evidence.

provenance.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Revised the description to retain supported academic scope and activities without superseded or unsupported details.

selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Introduction to World Archaeology
selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Introduction to World Archaeology explores craft production and material culture in ancient societies around the world. Students examine how making objects relates to religious, social and gendered identities, technologies and environmental effects. An experimental educational activity and discussion of contemporary archaeological methods connect interpretation with practice.

provenance.reviewNote: Compared with the current selected workbook field. Retained the existing description as a faithful account; updated its source provenance.

selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.name: African Art & Heritage
selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Examines the artistic, historical and ethical dimensions of African art. Highlights distinct forms and cultural significance, considers influence on Western modernism and addresses looting, colonial-era acquisitions and repatriation efforts.

selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Modern Art & Modern Museums
selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Examines debates on modern art through various themes. Focuses on the relationship between art and its presentation in museums and exhibitions, exploring curatorial practices and exhibition strategies.

selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Perspectives on Literary Meaning
selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Examines how different perspectives—humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural minority and psychoanalytic—affect reading and interpretation. Students undertake a research project applying selected perspectives to texts.

selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Introduction to Film & Media
selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Introduction to Film & Media examines how moving images create meaning through cinematography, editing, sound, narrative and performance. Film history connects early cinema and major movements with feminist and postcolonial interpretation, alongside television, digital platforms and spectatorship. An analytical or creative-analytical project combines close analysis, theory and scholarly research.

selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Media & the Environment
selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Examines representation of environmental concerns through visual culture. Explores the Anthropocene, animal representation, deep time, biocentrism, contested nature, indigenous and postcolonial media; analyzes how media shape environmental understanding; and includes a paper or media project.

selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.name: Media & Race
selectedSharedDescriptionReviews.text: Media & Race investigates storytelling, power, privilege, resistance and systemic racism in American history from the late nineteenth century to the present. Film, photographs, music and other media connect past and present. Students produce research-based podcasts exploring how media sustains oppression and supports resistance.
